title: Trump DHS Spied on Unions and Left-Wing Groups in Minnesota
description_short: Trump DHS Spied on Unions and Left-Wing Groups in Minnesota
description_medium: The linked report describes DHS surveillance during the 2026 federal occupation of Minneapolis and St. Paul, citing government documents reviewed by The New York Times and filed in federal court. It says agents infiltrated meetings, monitored encrypted chats, compiled personal dossiers, and sought financial records from unions and nonprofits. This account concerns the 2026 operation, not the 2020 protests described in the prior medium text.
description_long: The linked World Socialist Web Site report says government documents reviewed by The New York Times and made public in a federal court filing describe DHS surveillance during the 2026 federal occupation of Minneapolis and St. Paul. According to the report, undercover agents attended meetings in churches, libraries, parks, schools, restaurants, and union halls; recorded political discussions; entered encrypted Signal chats; collected license-plate information; and assembled dossiers containing names, photographs, home addresses, employment, and family details. The report also says Homeland Security Investigations used administrative summonses to obtain years of financial records from national unions and nonprofit organizations without identifying underlying criminal conduct. It characterizes the monitoring as directed at people protesting killings by federal immigration agents, the federal occupation, and the administration's deportation operation. The linked account attributes these details to government records reported by the New York Times; the packet does not include the filings themselves or a government response.

title: Pardons Glen Moss
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Glen Moss as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Donald Trump pardoned Glen Moss on January 19, 2021. The DOJ clemency list associates Moss with two federal cases: one in Connecticut involving payment to an unlicensed physician and tax evasion, and one in South Carolina involving mail fraud. It lists separate probation, home-confinement, fine, and restitution terms for the cases, but does not clarify which matters the pardon covered.
description_long: The Justice Department’s pardon list associates Glen Moss with two separate federal case histories. In Connecticut, it lists payment to a non-licensed physician and attempted tax evasion, with three years’ probation, a $4,000 fine, and a condition concerning unpaid taxes. In South Carolina, it lists mail fraud, five years’ probation, six months of home confinement, and $412,000 in restitution. The record identifies Trump’s pardon of Moss on January 19, 2021, but the table does not explain whether the grant covered both cases or provide its case-specific terms. Without a warrant or another official record, the scope of the pardon cannot be stated confidently. The listed offenses and sentences provide background, but they do not establish why Trump selected Moss or which obligations were affected. The clemency entry therefore has a confirmed recipient and date alongside a material ambiguity about the cases covered by the action.
notes: The linked DOJ list confirms the January 19, 2021 pardon and lists two case histories and their terms, but does not say which cases the warrant covered. The signed clemency instrument is still required to establish the scope and affected obligations.
